patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of sudden loss of consciousness with brief shaking movements
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Crawford is a 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, and prior anterior STEMI who presents to the emergency department after his third episode of sudden loss of consciousness in approximately six weeks. He was brought in by ambulance after collapsing at a grocery store approximately 90 minutes ago. A bystander witnessed the event and reported that the patient was standing in the checkout line when he suddenly dropped to the ground without any preceding stumble or warning cry. The witness describes that after falling, the patient exhibited brief jerking movements of his arms and legs lasting approximately 10-15 seconds, then lay still and appeared pale. He regained consciousness within approximately 30-40 seconds of the onset, was immediately conversational, and asked where he was. He denied any preceding lightheadedness, chest pain, palpitations, or aura. He did not bite his tongue and there was no urinary incontinence. By the time EMS arrived approximately 8 minutes later, the patient was sitting upright and reported feeling entirely normal. His two prior episodes occurred approximately six weeks ago and three weeks ago. The first event happened while he was watching television at home; he lost consciousness without warning and his neighbor, who was visiting, noted approximately 5 seconds of bilateral arm jerking before he spontaneously recovered. He did not seek medical attention for that episode. The second event occurred while climbing stairs in his apartment building; he suddenly blacked out, fell backwards down three stairs, and sustained a left elbow abrasion. Again, no prodrome, no post-ictal confusion beyond a brief period of disorientation lasting less than one minute, and no tongue biting or incontinence. He saw his primary care physician after the second event, who referred him for neurology evaluation with concern for new-onset seizures. He was seen briefly in a neurology clinic one week ago but no EEG had yet been performed. He reports increasing fatigue and exercise intolerance over the past several months, noting that he becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. He has not noticed palpitations but admits he has not been monitoring his pulse. He denies any recent medication changes, missed doses, fever, or acute illness.

general.query: cardiac syncope AV block trifascicular disease pacemaker indications
general.summary: Not retrieved on this pathway. Current ACC/AHA guidelines recommend Class I permanent pacemaker implantation for symptomatic Mobitz type II second-degree AV block and for trifascicular block with recurrent syncope. Correlate with current society guidelines.

pacemaker_medications.proposed: No new antiarrhythmic drug initiated on this pathway (pacemaker implantation is the intervention)
contraindications: Beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and adenosine: suppress AV conduction further in high-grade AV block — may precipitate complete heart block; avoid until pacemaker implanted.
warnings: Hydrochlorothiazide: should be held or discontinued given hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia which may aggravate conduction abnormalities.
Aspirin and clopidogrel: continue per cardiologist guidance post-pacemaker; no additional anticoagulation required for pacemaker alone.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Cardiac syncope due to paroxysmal high-grade (Mobitz II) AV block on a background of trifascicular conduction disease

differential.key_features: Prior anterior MI with anterior wall motion abnormality and PVCs is a substrate for VT; must be excluded by prolonged monitoring and EP study before attributing syncope to AV block alone.
Baseline sinus bradycardia at 51-54 bpm raises the possibility of intrinsic SA-node disease; SNRT on EP study and Holter help distinguish.
Witness-reported jerks lasting 10-15 s with no post-ictal confusion, no tongue bite, no incontinence, and normal EEG argue strongly against epilepsy and favor convulsive syncope.
No prodrome, no clear trigger, occurs in varied positions (seated TV-watching, climbing stairs); tilt-table negative.
Multiple antihypertensives including HCTZ raise the possibility, but events not positional and tilt-table shows no orthostatic drop.

sequence_constraints.reason: Disposition (admission vs discharge) and EP referral depend on ECG findings; ECG must be obtained first.
Troponin assessment for ACS should be available before committing to long-term monitoring strategy.
Structural assessment informs device strategy (pacemaker vs CRT/ICD).

critical_actions: Recognise bifascicular block plus first-degree AV block on ECG as trifascicular disease at risk of complete heart block
Place patient on continuous inpatient telemetry pending pacemaker evaluation
Consult cardiology/electrophysiology for permanent pacemaker indication
Counsel patient on driving restriction until syncope substrate is treated
Identify the witnessed brief limb jerking as convulsive syncope, not epilepsy, and avoid starting antiepileptic drugs
contraindicated_actions: Do not initiate antiepileptic drugs based on a misdiagnosis of convulsive syncope as seizure
Do not discharge home without prolonged cardiac monitoring or pacemaker plan
Do not administer further AV-nodal blockers (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, adenosine) until pacing is secured
Do not perform lumbar puncture — no clinical indication
Do not allow driving until pacemaker implant and physician clearance
key_reasoning_points: Bifascicular block + first-degree AV block on a resting ECG constitutes trifascicular disease and is a class I indication for inpatient monitoring and pacemaker consideration
Brief 10-15 s convulsive movements with rapid recovery, no tongue bite and no incontinence are characteristic of convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion, not epilepsy
A normal-rate baseline ECG does not exclude paroxysmal high-grade AV block — prolonged monitoring is essential to capture the responsible arrhythmia
Thiazide-induced hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia aggravate conduction system instability and should be corrected and HCTZ held
Prior anterior MI with PVCs raises the additional concern of monomorphic VT; EP study and ICD candidacy should be addressed alongside pacing
Driving must be restricted until the syncope substrate is definitively treated, given the public-safety risk of further episodes

red_herrings.data_point: Witnessed 10-15 s of arm and leg jerking
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be interpreted as a generalised tonic-clonic seizure and prompt EEG-led work-up only.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: These are myoclonic jerks from transient cerebral hypoperfusion (convulsive syncope); the EEG is normal and the arrhythmia substrate is on ECG/Holter.

red_herrings.intended_effect: May be taken to exclude epilepsy and shift focus away from the cardiac work-up unnecessarily.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A normal interictal EEG neither confirms nor excludes epilepsy and has no role in cardiac syncope diagnosis; the diagnostic data live on ECG and Holter.

red_herrings.intended_effect: May be invoked as 'anaemia-mediated' lightheadedness explaining all events.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild anaemia is insufficient to cause loss of consciousness without prodrome; the recorded paroxysmal AV block with 5.8 s pauses is the proximate cause.

clinical_pearls: Convulsive syncope (brief myoclonic jerks from cerebral hypoperfusion during syncope) is frequently misdiagnosed as epileptic seizure and is the most common cause of seizure misdiagnosis
Trifascicular block (bifascicular block + first-degree AV block) on ECG is a high-risk pattern that should prompt inpatient monitoring and cardiology consultation for pacemaker evaluation
Mobitz type II AV block is an infra-nodal block that characteristically does not improve with atropine or exercise, distinguishing it from Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) which is AV nodal
Exercise-induced worsening of AV block is pathognomonic for infra-Hisian disease, as AV nodal block improves with exercise due to increased sympathetic tone
Thiazide diuretics can cause hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, which may exacerbate cardiac conduction abnormalities
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 3 grounded red herrings (convulsive movements, normal EEG, mild anaemia), requires synthesis of ECG conduction-pattern recognition plus prolonged-monitoring yield over an apparently normal baseline rhythm.
